speaker: Vincent Clerc
title: The Potential of Data in Global Trade | Vincent Clerc
question: In maritime shipping, what is the economic logic behind charging a price on vessel emissions?
guest: The customer and society as a whole are already paying. It's not that by charging a price for emissions, internalizing externalities, or making the polluter pay that all of a sudden you have new costs. Already today, somebody else is paying for this—the people who live in Bangladesh and are flooded, or in Saint Lucia with hurricanes, or in Mali without crops, or in Switzerland without snow in the ski resorts. There are already people paying for climate change. The logical solution is to make the polluter pay, to make the right choice economically and commercially viable—to buy a ship that emits less, adopt alternative fuels, or do port call optimization. All of these things can be helped by data, but they need to be combined with the right incentives.

points.core: Society already bears externalized climate damages before any emissions price exists.
points.note: Accept: climate costs are already being paid today by affected populations/society (flooding, storms, crop loss, etc.). Do not credit: generic statements that "climate change is bad" without framing it as an existing unpriced cost.

points.core: Carbon pricing internalizes existing externalities onto polluters rather than creating new costs.
points.note: Accept: polluter-pays principle reallocating existing externalized costs onto emitters rather than inventing brand-new societal costs. Do not credit: treating carbon pricing purely as a tax/penalty without the cost-internalization mechanism.

points.core: Pricing emissions makes lower-emission ships commercially viable for fleet operators.
points.note: Accept: making low-emission vessels, alternative fuels, or port call optimization economically worthwhile/competitive. Do not credit: generic statements that pricing "encourages sustainability" without commercial viability.

points.core: Operational data requires aligned financial incentives to actually drive emissions reductions.
points.note: Accept: data and optimization tools alone are insufficient without economic/pricing incentives to adopt them. Do not credit: claims that data visibility by itself solves decarbonization.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core logic is correcting an externality. Ships burning heavy fuel oil impose costs on others, through climate damage from CO2 and health harms from sulphur and particulates, that the shipowner and cargo customers don't pay. Because those costs are missing from freight rates, the market produces more emissions than is socially efficient. A price on emissions (a levy per tonne of CO2, or tradable allowances as in the EU Emissions Trading System, which has covered shipping since 2024) makes the polluter bear that cost.

Three effects follow. First, it narrows the cost gap between cheap fossil bunker fuel and much more expensive low-carbon alternatives such as green methanol or ammonia, making investment in them commercially viable. Second, it rewards every abatement option without regulators picking winners: slow steaming, hull and engine efficiency, wind assistance, route optimisation. Operators choose whatever is cheapest for them, so a given emissions cut is achieved at the lowest overall cost. Third, it raises revenue, which can fund clean-fuel deployment or compensate developing countries facing higher trade costs.

Because shipping is global and mobile, a uniform international price also limits evasion and preserves a level competitive playing field.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Charging a price on vessel emissions corrects a classic market failure by internalizing the negative externalities of climate damage and air pollution. Because conventional marine fuels like heavy fuel oil do not reflect their full social cost, zero- and near-zero-emission alternatives such as green methanol or ammonia remain commercially uncompetitive. Putting an explicit price on emissions narrows or closes this fuel cost gap, aligning private commercial incentives with societal costs.

Unlike prescriptive technical mandates, emissions pricing drives cost-effective abatement across a diverse global fleet. Operators have the flexibility to cut emissions wherever doing so costs less than paying the carbon price—whether through immediate operational adjustments like slow steaming and route optimization, energy-saving retrofits such as wind-assisted propulsion, or long-term capital investments in clean-fuel vessels. This price signal also flows through supply chains, rewarding cleaner carriers and helping resolve split incentives between shipowners who fund efficiency upgrades and charterers who pay for fuel. Finally, levies or allowance auctions generate revenues that can subsidize early-stage clean fuels, finance port bunkering infrastructure, and support an equitable transition for developing economies.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main idea is to correct an externality. When ships burn heavy fuel oil, they release CO₂ and other pollutants that harm the climate and public health. Shipowners and charterers don't pay for that harm, so fossil fuel looks cheaper than it really is to society, and the industry emits more than it would if it paid the full cost. A price per tonne of emissions, set as a carbon tax or levy or through an emissions trading scheme such as the EU ETS, which has covered shipping since 2024, puts that cost into the operator's own decisions.

That price then works on every margin at once. Operators can slow-steam, optimise routes, retrofit hulls and engines, order more efficient ships, or switch to fuels like ammonia, methanol or biofuels. Each firm cuts emissions where it can do so most cheaply, so the system reaches a given target at lower total cost than one-size-fits-all rules. A predictable price also narrows the cost gap with zero-emission fuels, which encourages long-term investment in them. Revenue from the levy can fund research or help vulnerable developing economies.

Because shipping is global and ships can easily switch their flag registration, a uniform international price, like the one negotiated at the IMO, limits evasion and keeps competition fair.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Charging a price on vessel emissions rests on the economic principle of internalizing a negative externality. Historically, maritime shipping has emitted greenhouse gases without paying for the climate damages those emissions cause, leaving conventional fossil bunker fuels artificially cheap relative to their true social cost. Putting a price on emissions—through a fuel levy, feebate, or emissions trading system—corrects this market failure by building environmental costs directly into operating expenses. In the short term, this gives carriers a flexible financial incentive to cut fuel burn through the lowest-cost measures available, such as slow steaming, route optimization, and energy-saving retrofits. Over the longer term, it narrows the substantial price gap between fossil fuels and cleaner alternatives like green methanol or ammonia, providing shipowners, fuel producers, and ports with the predictable price signal needed to invest in low-emission vessels and bunkering infrastructure. Finally, the resulting revenues can be recycled to support early adopters, fund clean-technology development, and offset higher freight costs for vulnerable developing economies.

Pricing vessel emissions makes shipping companies pay for some of the climate damage their operations impose on society. Without a price, shipowners pay for fuel, but the harm from burning it is largely borne by others. A charge per tonne of greenhouse gas emitted brings that cost into decisions about how ships are operated, fueled, and built.

The price gives operators a reason to cut emissions wherever doing so costs less than paying the charge. One ship might save fuel by sailing more slowly, while another might invest in a more efficient engine or switch to a cleaner fuel. This flexibility directs emissions cuts toward the lowest-cost options and gives companies a financial reason to invest in cleaner ships and fuels.

A common price lets carriers choose the cheapest reductions across the fleet. To the extent that carriers pass the charge on, freight rates also give shippers a reason to choose lower-emission transport.
